title: What r Cannot See
scopeNote: This keeps the live scatter with a correlation computed on the points actually drawn, and the movable observation. The negative and zero relationship presets, the change-of-units demonstration and the guess-the-correlation challenge set stay in the longer version, and the page says so.
summary: Twenty-four fixed observations and one the learner can move anywhere. Two fitted lines are drawn, through all twenty-five points and through the other twenty-four, so a single point's influence is visible as a gap rather than only as a change in a number.
learningObjectives: State what r measures, and that the word straight is doing the work.
Recognise that a strong curved relationship can produce an r near zero.
Recognise that one observation out of twenty-five can create or destroy a correlation.
Distinguish an unusual observation from an influential one, and explain what leverage depends on.
Explain why a scatter plot must be inspected before a correlation is interpreted.
interactionTypes: a three-option pattern switch with all labels permanently visible
two range inputs positioning a single observation anywhere on the plane
a live scatter with correlations computed on the points actually drawn
two fitted lines, with and without the movable point, and a key
a four-part challenge walking the linearity and leverage cases
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Everything is computed in the browser and is gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. The movable observation is controlled by two labelled range inputs rather than by dragging, which is deliberate: a drag target is hard to operate from a keyboard and cannot report its position. The pattern switch is a radio group with all three labels permanently visible. The two fitted lines differ by dash pattern as well as colour and are named in a key carrying a sample of each, placed clear of the plot so it cannot collide with an axis label. The figure description gives the shape of the cloud, the movable point's position, both correlations and both slopes. The figure scrolls sideways rather than shrinking below legible label sizes on a narrow screen. Changes are announced through a polite live region. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Simulated and illustrative. The twenty-four fixed observations are generated in the browser from constant seeds, so every learner sees the same cloud and a lecturer can quote the same numbers. Variable X and Variable Y are deliberately unnamed: nothing here is real data.
simulationNotes: The plot area is square and both axes are fixed at 0 to 100. Both decisions matter. The apparent strength of a correlation depends on the aspect ratio it is drawn at, so a stretched plot would flatter a weak relationship; and the movable point must move within a stable frame, or the learner cannot tell whether the picture changed because the point moved or because the plot rescaled. The shapeless cloud has its own seed and its own tighter spread, chosen by sweeping candidates for two properties at once: the twenty-four points alone correlate minus 0.0007, which is genuinely nothing rather than a small chance trend, and they sit compactly enough that the single movable point has real leverage. Placed in the top corner it takes r to plus 0.52; placed in the bottom corner, to minus 0.44. A wide cloud would have made the demonstration limp.
readmeTopic: what a correlation coefficient measures, what it cannot see, and how much one observation can move it
